title: City Lights
synopsis: A tramp, a blind flower girl, a drunken millionaire who only remembers you at night, and a small coin that decides everything.

nodes.text: The tarp comes off the new monument and there you are, curled asleep in the marble lap of Peace and Prosperity. A brass band stops mid-note. Officials go the color of the ribbon. You climb down by way of a stone sword, and the sword catches you by the seat of your trousers, and holds.

choices.consequence: You come to attention on a stone thigh, hand at your hat brim, while the anthem plays and a policeman below turns purple.
You get down in stages, one of them involving a bronze face, and land in the flowerbed like a man who meant it.

nodes.text: She holds violets out to the whole street, and you take one, and your last coin goes into her palm. A limousine door slams behind you. She hears the door, and turns her face toward it, and says thank you, sir — to a car that has already left with somebody else in it.

choices.consequence: You spend the coin you were going to eat with. The violet costs you supper, and you would do it again before lunch.
You get four steps down the pavement and come back, because she is still holding the flower out to nobody at all.

nodes.text: A gentleman on the riverwall is tying a brick to his neck with the care of a man knotting a tie. You mime that life is worth living. He weeps. He embraces you. The rope is around his neck and now also around yours, and the brick is already in the water.

choices.consequence: You go in twice and come out twice, and he saves you the second time, and neither of you can swim particularly well.
You offer the violet instead of an argument. He looks at it a long moment, then at the river, then decides on the flower.

nodes.text: He calls you his friend for life and drives you home himself, at speed, on both sides of the road. In the marble hall he hands you a cigar, a caviar spoon, and his car. You sit in a chair built for a man twice your size, holding a cigar as long as your forearm, being loved enormously.

choices.consequence: You accept a guest room with a bed the size of a barge, and sleep on the floor beside it, because the bed is too much.
You reach for your hat and he blocks the door with his whole body and his whole heart, so you stay until breakfast.

nodes.text: Daylight. He comes down the stairs pressed and combed and looks at you the way you would look at a stain. Who let this in. The butler takes your elbow with two fingers, as though you might be sticky, and the front door opens onto a very bright street, and closes.

choices.consequence: You lift your hat to a man who has forgotten you exist, straighten your collar on the step, and go and find work.
You point at the cigar box, the car, the chair. The butler nods along politely and keeps walking you backwards toward the kerb.

nodes.text: Through her window you watch the landlord hold up a slip of paper she cannot read, and say the number out loud twice, and leave. Her grandmother stirs a pot of something mostly water. The girl smiles the entire time. She has not once let anyone see her count the flowers she did not sell.

choices.consequence: You turn out your pockets on the kerb: one button, one bent nail, a tram ticket. You will have the rent by Friday or invent it.
You stand in the alley until the lamplighter passes, working out what a man can earn in four days starting from nothing at all.

nodes.text: The arrangement is simple: your opponent carries you two rounds and you split the purse. Then he leaves town ahead of a warrant, and the man who replaces him is a slab with a neck. He shadowboxes in the corner. The bag he is hitting has stopped swinging, out of respect.

choices.consequence: You plan to go down early and gracefully. The plan survives until his first swing misses and knocks your hat clean across the ring.
You decide the girl's rent will be won cleanly, which is a beautiful sentiment and an extremely poor piece of arithmetic.

nodes.text: You discover the referee. Wherever the big man goes, you go behind the referee, and the three of you cross the canvas like a slow dance nobody rehearsed. The crowd is delighted. The bell rope catches your collar on the turn and hauls you up onto your toes, ringing steadily, keeping time.

choices.consequence: You use a licensed official as furniture for a round and a half, until the crowd starts placing bets on the referee.
You land one. It is a good one. He blinks, considers it briefly, and files it away somewhere under weather.

nodes.text: No purse, no prize, and a lip you can feel with your tongue. The last car of the night stands lit at the corner with its bell going, and the fare is a nickel, and you have a button. The conductor watches you count the button twice, in case it turns into something.

choices.consequence: Forty blocks in shoes that stopped being shoes in March. You arrive at dawn with your hat brushed and your posture excellent.
You ride the rear step six stops before the conductor spots you, then dismount at speed into a hedge, hat still on.

nodes.text: The horn goes twice. There he is, hanging out of the window, delighted, calling you brother across the whole avenue — champagne-certain you are the finest man he has ever met. Sober, he does not know your face. Drunk, he would give you the city. Your fortunes now depend entirely on his liver.

choices.consequence: You take the money for a girl who will never learn where it came from. You do not feel clean about it. You take it.
You push the notes back twice. He pushes harder, wounded, insisting — and a friendship this loud cannot be declined in public.

nodes.text: Two men come through the study window while he is counting the notes onto the rug for you. One of them has a sap. Your host goes down across the fireplace inside four seconds, still smiling. You are alone in a dark room with a thousand dollars, two burglars, and a poker you are holding backwards.

choices.consequence: You go at two grown criminals with a fire iron, which is brave, and you swing it, which is loud, and the window is still open.

choices.text: Save the cash for the girl
choices.consequence: You get the notes inside your shirt before you get to the door. The thieves leave one way and you leave the other.

nodes.text: The officers arrive and find one unconscious millionaire, one open safe, and you, with a thousand dollars stuffed down your front and no explanation available in mime. Your host sits up, blinks, and looks at you with polite confusion. He has never seen you before in his life. Again.

choices.consequence: You duck under an officer's arm and take the long way round, because a girl across town needs this money before morning.
You act the entire burglary out — window, sap, two men — with tremendous accuracy, to a sergeant writing down your hat size.

nodes.text: The clipping is folded soft from handling: a Viennese surgeon, a procedure, a figure with three digits. Her grandmother keeps it under the sugar tin and has never once said it out loud. You have a thousand dollars against your ribs and about four minutes before somebody knocks on that door.

choices.consequence: You put the whole sum into her hands and keep nothing back, not even carfare, and wave it off as a small matter.
You count out the arrears first so nobody can put her on the street while she is bandaged, then push the rest across the table.

nodes.text: The stairwell is dark and the pencil is a stub. You cannot say it, so you write it, badly, twice, and slide the paper under her door. It says you are going away on business. It does not say where. Her grandmother will read it aloud tonight, in a voice that makes it sound like a better lie than it is.

choices.consequence: You put your name on it in careful capitals, so that whatever happens next, she knows exactly who it was.
You leave it unsigned. Let her think a stranger was kind to her; strangers are allowed to disappear without explaining themselves.

nodes.text: The sentence is read out to a room of nine people, none of whom are there for you. Inside they give you a number, a tin cup, and a job sewing mailbags. You turn out to be very good at sewing mailbags. It is the first thing this city has ever let you finish.

choices.consequence: You serve the months quietly with the newspaper clipping folded inside your shoe, and take it out on Sundays to look at.
You try to name the two men who came through the window. Nobody writes it down. The mailbags still need sewing.

nodes.text: They give you back your hat, your cane, and a coat that has given up in the shoulders. The corner where she sold violets is a shoe repair now. Two newsboys look at you the way boys look at something that has stopped being a person, and one of them fires a pea at your neck.

choices.consequence: You start asking after a flower girl, and every answer moves you one street further west, toward a window with a striped awning.
You keep walking, because a man in this coat has no business looking for anybody, and your feet turn west without consulting you.

nodes.text: Plate glass, a striped awning, roses standing in tin buckets. She is at the counter arranging stems, and she is looking at them — actually looking, head tilted, choosing. A woman beside her says something, and the two of them laugh at a man on the pavement with a pea-shot on his collar.

choices.consequence: You straighten what is left of your tie in the reflection and step toward the door, which is the bravest thing you have done sober.
You stay at the kerb picking a flower out of the gutter, telling yourself you only wanted to know that she was all right.

nodes.text: She comes out with a fresh rose and a quarter, the way you hand things to a man you feel sorry for. Her friend holds the door. You press the flower to your chest with both hands and try to give the coin back, and she folds your fingers over it, laughing kindly.

choices.consequence: You accept charity from the person you went to prison for, and you thank her for it, and you mean the thank you.
You push the coin back and she pushes harder, and for four seconds you are two people arguing over a quarter in broad daylight.

nodes.text: Her thumb goes across your knuckles the way it used to, back when hands were the only thing she had. She stops. Her face does something very small. She takes your hand in both of hers and reads it — the callus, the tendon, the exact width of the wrist she once held to say goodbye.

choices.consequence: You do not move a finger. Whatever she is about to find out, you are not going to make her chase you for it.
You start to pull away and manage an inch, and she holds on, and that inch is the last thing you had left to give.

nodes.text: You? Her mouth is still trying for a joke and her eyes have already given it up. Behind her the shop is warm and crowded with stems in water, and in front of her stands a man with a pea-shot on his collar, holding a rose like a hymn book.

choices.consequence: You nod once, small, and let her have the whole answer at once, and you do not take any of it back afterwards.
You study the pavement rather than let her watch your face do what it is doing, and she stands there and waits you out.

nodes.text: Nothing moves on the street. She is holding your hand against the front of her coat, and you have two fingers at your mouth, doing the thing you do when you cannot speak, which is always. The whole picture is one expression wide. Everything either of you has is in the next second.

choices.consequence: You let it out — the entire smile, the one you have been saving since the corner with the violets — and she does not let go.
You lower your eyes and try to slide your hand loose, already composing the exit, already apologizing for turning out to be the answer.
There is a version of this where nobody has to say anything at all, and it has been waiting on this pavement all afternoon.

nodes.text: She closes both hands over yours and laughs, and the laugh has a crack straight down the middle of it. Her friend, in the doorway, decides to go and count something in the back room. The shop smells of gardenia and wet paper. You stand there holding a rose you were given for free, being looked at, all the way, for the first time in your life.

You take your hand back gently, lift your hat, and go before she has to decide anything. The bell over her door rings twice behind you. At the corner you look at the rose, put it in your buttonhole, and square your shoulders, because there is a whole city ahead and it is a fine afternoon. The pavement stays empty a long time after you leave the frame.

You become the man who sweeps her step on Tuesdays, takes no wages, and gives a false name that changes slightly every year. She marries a decent man who sells sheet music. Decades on, clearing a drawer, she finds a surgeon's receipt made out in careful capitals to a name she has heard a hundred times over a broom, and sits down on her own shop floor.
